ch12 - Richness and diversity in Indian thought.md
chapters.relation: Argues that in India philosophy and religion were never separated as the post-Kantian West separates them: philosophizing is a soteriological quest in which understanding the nature of reality directly affects one's destiny, more comparable to Socrates' quest for wisdom than to modern academic philosophy. It introduces the framework of darshanas ('views' of reality taught by seers), the claim that disciplined mental exercises can yield yogic perception of metaphysical truth, and karma-rebirth as the shared Indian worldview, contrasting ritual-correctness karma with the Buddha's radically intention-based version and discussing verbal testimony as an everyday but religiously unchecked means of knowledge. It closes by delimiting the book's scope (the six classical darshanas plus Buddhism; Jainism, Carvaka, and Shaivism omitted) and warning against the Western habit of romanticizing Indian thought as mystical rather than recognizing its strong rational-debate tradition. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

Presents the two coexisting branches of the Brahmanical tradition around 500 BCE: the Vedic sacrificial religion, in which precisely performed ritual actions (physical and verbal karma) maintained cosmic order (dharma) and underwrote brahmin social authority, and the Upanishadic internalization of the sacrifice. The Upanishads shift the focus to the person, teaching that experiential insight into the identity of one's essential self (atman) and the cosmos (Brahman) - 'tat tvam asi' - brings moksha from rebirth, illustrated with the Rig Veda 10.129 creation hymn and passages from the Chandogya and Brihadaranyaka Upanishads. It carefully distinguishes monism (one existent thing) from monotheism, sets the Upanishadic oneness against the pluralistic realism of the ritualists, and shows how this internal tension became the fault line along which later Indian philosophical debate would run. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

Reconstructs the Buddha's teaching as a Middle Way on three levels: socially between householder ritualism and renouncer asceticism, in monastic life between indulgence and austerities, and metaphysically between every permutation of existence and non-existence. It details the Enlightenment's three insights, the Four Noble Truths (dukkha better rendered 'unsatisfactoriness' grounded in the impermanence of all conditioned things), and dependent origination as the 'regularity of things'. Against the standard reading of anatta as 'there is no self', it argues the Buddha denied only independent existence and shifted inquiry from ontology to the workings of the cognitive apparatus (the five khandhas), citing his refusal to answer the Unanswered Questions. It also gives the Buddha's specific critiques of brahmin claims to authority, the purposelessness of ritual, and reliance on tradition over one's own experience. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

Shows how the brahmins defended the Veda against fifth-century challenges by formalizing the study of language: Panini's grammar codified the ritually creative Sanskrit whose sounded sentences (e.g. 'water wets grain') were held to bring about their effects impersonally, and Patanjali and Katyayana's 'usage' criterion allowed awkward or conflicting Vedic passages to be read as metaphor, preserving the text's coherence. It then presents Jaimini's Mimamsa Sutra reading of the Veda purely as injunctions - dharma defined as 'what should be done' - with word-meaning taken to guarantee the existence of what words designate, so that the Veda validates both the plural cosmos and the ritual agents who maintain it; the Upanishadic monist passages are defused as metaphor. Finally it presents Badarayana's Vedanta (Brahma) Sutra pivoting instead to 'enquiry into Brahman', and shows how both exegetes established testimony (shabda-pramana) as a lasting and contested Indian means of knowledge, alongside the purva-paksha style of stating an opponent's view before refuting it. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

Exposes Kanada's Vaisheshika pluralistic realism: seven categories (substance, quality, action, universality, particularity, inherence, and absence) and nine eternal substances, with earth, water, fire, and air atoms combining to form all composite objects - the red of a red rose illustrating quality, inherence, universality, and particularity. It then presents Gotama's Nyaya contribution: a formal five-membered inferential method (thesis, reason, example, application, conclusion - 'there is fire on the hill because there is smoke') grounded in perception and invariable rules rather than Vedic testimony, plus criteria (doubt, purpose, possibility of certainty) for when enquiry is legitimate. Nyaya uses this method to 'prove' a plurality of eternal selves from the plurality of consciousnesses and their qualities, and the chapter notes the standing modern comparison of the method with Aristotle's syllogism. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

Traces Buddhist scholasticism from the eighteen early schools (Lokottaravadins, Sammatiyas, Sautrantikas, Sarvastivadins, with Theravada the survivor) through the Abhidharma projects - Sarvastivada dharmas existing in all three time modes with an essence (svabhava), Theravada's categorization of some 28 physical and 52 mental dharmas - and their critique of Nyaya-Vaisheshika partless atoms. It then presents the Mahayana response: the Perfection of Wisdom sutras' teaching that all dharmas are empty of own-being, and Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka demonstration that nothing with own-being can arise from itself, from another, from both, or spontaneously, together with his two truths (conventional and ultimate) and the 'emptiness of emptiness' - emptiness affirms, rather than denies, the dependently originated world, since without it no change or knowledge would be possible. It closes with Vasubandhu's Yogacara 'Mind-Only' analysis of transformations of consciousness, karmic 'seeds' in a storehouse consciousness, and the constructed, dependent, and perfected aspects of experience, which denies that perception establishes the external existence of its objects. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

Presents Classical Yoga's Yoga Sutras as above all a practice manual for 'the cessation of the activities of the mind' (citta-vritti-nirodha), through which the practitioner discriminates the conscious but inactive witness (purusha) from unconscious, active manifest nature (prakriti) - delusion consisting in mistaking the manifest ego for the conscious self - and discusses the ambiguous status of the 'Lord' (Ishvara) verses. It then presents Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika as the matching dualist ontology: numerically plural but ontologically identical purushas versus one prakriti colored by the three qualities of goodness, passion, and inertia, enumerated through categories from buddhi (will/discernment) and the 'I-maker' (ahamkara) down to the gross elements, with satkaryavada (the effect pre-exists in the cause) argued by inference. It highlights the startling Samkhya conclusion that 'nothing really is bound; no-one is reborn and no-one is released', since only prakriti ever cycles, and closes with Hamilton's own suggestion that prakriti's manifestation may describe a cognition-dependent world of experience rather than material nature. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

Covers the later grammatical and exegetical schools: Bhartrhari's claim that the whole sentence is the unit of meaning, that there is no knowledge without language, and that reality is a continuous indivisible 'sound-Brahman' (shabda-Brahman) knowable through grammar; the Mimamsakas (Kumarila and Prabhakara) defending the eternal, authorless Veda as injunction, holding cognition itself intrinsically reliable so that knowing reveals both the plural external world and the autonomous agent-selves who perform the sacrifice (with an 'identity in difference' category analysis and visible-sized atoms). It then presents Vedanta: Shankara's Advaita monism in which atman is Brahman, plurality has only conventional reality (the coiled rope mistaken for a snake; the trees seeming to move to a boatman), ignorance rather than Brahman causes the world of appearance, and Shankara remains a theistic monist despite his 'crypto-Buddhist' critics; versus Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita, in which Brahman really transforms itself into the qualified, plural world (parinama-vada) and selves relate to the Lord as redness to a rose - eternally inseparable yet distinct. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

chapters.file: ch20 - From Classical Thought to the Modern Day.md
chapters.relation: A historical postscript arguing that the classical period of Indian thought (some 1500 years, peaking in the first five centuries CE) ended amid massive textual loss and a tradition that kept almost no historical records, leaving chronology and authorship largely conjectural; Buddhism survived only outside India, and devotional traditions and a 'new' Nyaya outlived the great debating schools. It credits nineteenth-century Western Indology with both making the material accessible and imposing 'Western/Christian eyes', and argues that modern university-based revival has unfortunately reduced Indian philosophy to logic and linguistic analysis to compete on Western terms - abstraction from the soteriological context being, it says, a wholly Western cultural phenomenon. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

holes.name: Darshana (philosophical 'view' or school)
holes.what: In the Indian tradition a darshana is a systematic 'view' of the truth about reality taught by a lineage of seers (rishis), combining ontology and epistemology with a soteriological practice aimed at liberation.
holes.why: Chapter 12 makes darshana the organizing framework of the entire Indian tradition (the six classical schools are all darshanas), and the book's structure is built around them, but taxonomy has no equivalent.

holes.name: Vedic Sacrifice (yajna)
holes.what: The Brahmanical ritual religion in which brahmin priests, through precisely performed fire sacrifices with chanted Sanskrit formulas, maintained cosmic order (dharma) on behalf of society.
holes.why: Chapter 13's first half is an exposition of this sacrificial religion and its karma-as-ritual-action mechanics, which are the soil from which Indian philosophy grows, yet taxonomy covers no Vedic material.

holes.name: Dependent Origination (pratityasamutpada)
holes.what: The Buddha's teaching that all phenomena arise in mutual dependence on conditions - 'when this is, that is' - so that nothing exists independently, underlying both impermanence and not-self.
holes.why: Chapter 14 presents dependent origination as the most radical of the Buddha's teachings and the key to the Middle Way, and chapter 17 builds Nagarjuna's entire emptiness doctrine on it, but taxonomy has no slug for it.

holes.name: Panini
holes.what: Fourth-century BCE grammarian whose Astadhyayi, some 4000 rules, codified classical Sanskrit in one of the most sophisticated grammars in the history of linguistics.
holes.why: Chapter 15's whole defense of the Veda through language rests on Panini's grammar and the doctrine that ritually sounded Sanskrit is creatively efficacious; he is a central figure with no taxonomy presence.

holes.name: Vaisheshika Categories (padartha)
holes.what: Kanada's pluralistic-realist ontology of seven categories - substance, quality, action, universality, particularity, inherence, and absence - with all substance reducible to nine eternal kinds including atoms.
holes.why: Chapter 16 is largely a detailed exposition of this categorial system, which supplied the ontology for the whole Nyaya-Vaisheshika school, and nothing in taxonomy covers it beyond the loose analogy of Greek atomism.

holes.name: Nyaya Five-Membered Inference (anviksiki)
holes.what: The Nyaya school's formal logical method - thesis, reason, example, application, conclusion, as in 'there is fire on the hill because there is smoke' - grounded in perception and invariable concomitance.
holes.why: Chapter 16 presents this as the first formal philosophical method in India and the core of Nyaya's epistemology of pramanas; taxonomy has no entry for Indian logic.

holes.name: Abhidharma (Buddhist dharma analysis)
holes.what: The scholastic Buddhist tradition of defining the teachings and categorizing all phenomena (dharmas) - e.g. Theravada's 80-odd kinds and Sarvastivada's time-transcending dharmas with own-being (svabhava).
holes.why: Chapter 17's first half is devoted to the Abhidharma schools and their reification of dharmas, which is precisely what Nagarjuna's emptiness critique targets; taxonomy lacks any coverage of it.

holes.name: Yogacara 'Mind-Only' (cittamatra)
holes.what: The Buddhist school of Asanga and Vasubandhu analyzing experience as transformations of consciousness - karmic 'seeds' in a storehouse consciousness constructing the subject-object world, with constructed, dependent, and perfected aspects.
holes.why: Chapter 17 gives an extended account of this consciousness-only idealism as the alternative to Madhyamaka, and taxonomy has no slug for it or for Buddhist idealism generally.

holes.name: Classical Yoga (Patanjali's Yoga Sutra)
holes.what: The darshana codified in the Yoga Sutras: a methodology for the cessation of the activities of the mind (citta-vritti-nirodha) that discriminates the conscious witness (purusha) from unconscious nature (prakriti).
holes.why: Chapter 18 is devoted to it and its companion Samkhya ontology, and taxonomy's only yoga-adjacent entries are unrelated; yoga as a philosophical system is entirely missing.

holes.name: Samkhya Dualism (purusha and prakriti)
holes.what: The ontology of Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika: numerically plural, inactive, conscious purushas versus one eternal, active, unconscious prakriti manifest through the three gunas, with liberation as their discrimination.
holes.why: Chapter 18's second half expounds this dualism (including satkaryavada and the 'I-maker'), which is one of the six classical darshanas and the stated ontological partner of Classical Yoga; taxonomy has no entry.

holes.name: Ramanuja
holes.what: Eleventh-century Vedantin of the Sri Vaishnava devotional tradition whose Vishishtadvaita ('qualified non-dualism') holds that Brahman really transforms into the qualified plural world and that selves are eternally inseparable from the Lord.
holes.why: Chapter 19 gives Ramanuja's system equal billing with Shankara's Advaita as the major Vedanta, noting it is more representative of ordinary Hindu belief, but taxonomy includes only Shankara.

holes.name: Mimamsa (Vedic exegesis)
holes.what: The darshana, from Jaimini through Kumarila and Prabhakara, defending the eternal authorless Veda as injunction, cognition as intrinsically self-validating, and a plural world of agent-selves who maintain dharma through sacrifice.
holes.why: Chapters 15 and 19 treat Mimamsa as the orthodox pole of Indian epistemology and ontology (word meaning guaranteeing existence, self-validating cognition), and taxonomy has no entry for this school or its epistemology.
